content.title: This paper presents an interesting new method to learn word alignments but rely on wrong assumptions. This methods may work reasonably well for close language pairs but the evaluation lack of experiments on distant language pairs that may show some strong limits of the proposed method.
content.review:
This paper presents an interesting new method to learn word alignments based on neural networks. It is claimed unsupervised, with better or similar performance with previous work, and faster.


Strengths:
- the method is well presented and easy to understand
- results (AER) on European language pairs are convincing that the method can perform reasonably well for such language pairs.

Weaknesses:
- the main weakness of the proposed method is that it relies on the very strong and wrong assumption that word alignments are "mirror-like" symmetric. The paper does not discuss the problem of fertility (how does the method learn alignments for word aligned with several words) and the NULL alignment (word aligned with no other words as it may happen relatively often in a sentence aligned corpus that usually also contains translation errors). I assume that the method can successfully mitigate these problems for relatively close European language pairs, as shown in the experiments, but may dramatically fail for much more distant language pairs with very high fertility and for which word alignment is much more difficult (Japanese-English for instance).
- the method is evaluated only for somewhat close languages while it is well known that word alignments methods that may work well for European language pairs may poorly perform on distant language pairs (for instance, the original version of fast-align)
- the speeds comparison between GPU-based and CPU-based methods is not convincing. GIZA and fast-align can both be easily multi-threaded, while mgiza is not very efficient on exploiting multiple CPU, fast-align is much faster. I think the comparison is not fair regarding the cost of buying/running one CPU against one GPU and that clusters for computing are still all equipped with CPUs. I think nobody is currently still running giza or fast-align on a single CPU. It makes this setting rather artificial.


To improve the paper, I recommend the following:
- introducing at least one distant language pair in the evaluation (e.g., European-Asian languages)
- thorough discussion about the fertility problem and how the proposed method is addressing it.
- running the multi-threaded version of GIZA and fast-align to make a realistic speed comparison.



questions:
- does using sentence alignment not make the proposed method supervised? I do not know about previous work dubbing this requirement as still being unsupervised but it seems wrong since the method exploit alignment knowledge, at sentence-level, provided by humans. If this is right, how should we qualify a method that does not use any human alignment knowledge? I think "unsupervised" is unnecessary and may be confusing in this paper.
- section 1: is word alignment really easier than translation? I am not sure about this. Do you have any reference to cite?
- comparing speed between giza/fast-align and NN methods is very difficult as they exploit different computing devices. Any attempt to run them on multiple CPU and GPU, respectively? I actually expect fast-align to be much faster than what is reported in the paper.
- section 2: why "almost" the fastest for fast-align? Any references for faster methods?
- why did you chose grow-diag heuristic? In SMT, for instance, grow-diag-final-and usually shows much better results.
- in section 4.3, MirrorAlign is trained on K80 while in section 4.5 it is trained on P40, is this correct? If so, why changing the GPU?

Style:
- order reference citations chronoligically (abstract)
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer #4
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments. We summarize and reply to your questions as follows.

**Q1:** Wrong assumption that word alignments are "mirror-like" symmetric. How the proposed method addresses the fertility problem?

**A1:** We noticed that this question is your primary concern for our paper. **Actually, Such a “mirror-like” symmetric is the agreement hypothesis (Liang et al., 2006), which is well proved in the field of statistical machine translation and is referred to in section 3.3.**  We call it “mirror-like” in some part of our article because of that hypothesis and our strictly symmetric model architecture. We sincerely hope you can agree with our naming and reconsider the scoring of our article.

For the fertility problem, the current mainstream method (Zenkel et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Zenkel et al., 2020) is using BPE to handle the one-to-multi problem (namely, we consider each target word as being aligned to a source word if an alignment between any of the target subwords and source subwords exists.) and we followed this setting. We will highlight it in our paper to prevent misunderstanding. For the NULL alignment problem, as I know there is no good solution when induction alignments from an attention map. Possibly limiting the threshold in the attention map is a solution, but we have not made such attempts. 

----

**Q2:** Introducing at least one distant language pair in the evaluation. The method may dramatically fail for much more distant language pairs with very high fertility and for which word alignment is much more difficult (Japanese-English for instance).

**A2:** We noticed that the fertility problem is your biggest concern to our model about the long-distance language problem, and you can find the answer in **A1**. 


----

**Q3:** Does using sentence alignment not make the proposed method supervised? If this is right, how should we qualify a method that does not use any human alignment knowledge?

**A3:** “Unsupervised” here means that no artificially labeled word alignment information is used in training.

----

**Q4:** Any attempt to run them on multiple CPU and GPU, respectively?  

**A4:** The comparison is conducted on one multi-threaded CPU for fastalign and GIZA++ and one GPU for our model respectively. 

----

**Q5:** Section 1: is word alignment really easier than translation? I am not sure about this. Do you have any references to cite?

**A5:** Intuitively, the problem space of word alignment is much smaller than that of translation. For word alignment, the model only needs to point out the correspondence between the given source and target words. Empirically, in the field of SMT, the alignment model is a prerequisite, which means the MT task is much more complex too. 

----

**Q6:** Why did you choose the grow-diag heuristic? In SMT, for instance, grow-diag-final-and usually shows much better results.

**A6:** We try both of them and choose the better performance one to report. Many other neural alignment models(Garg et al., 2019; Zenkel et al., 2019; Zenkel et al., 2020) achieve the best results on the grow-diag heuristic too. 

----

**Q7:** in section 4.3, MirrorAlign is trained on K80 while in section 4.5 it is trained on P40, is this correct? If so, why change the GPU?

**A7:** Thanks for your suggestion. That’s our mistake. We trained our model on P40 at last. We will correct it in the next version.

----

**Q8:** Order reference citations chronologically (abstract)

**A8:** Thanks for your suggestion. We will correct it in the next version.

----

We keenly hope that you can re-evaluate our work based on our response.

content.title: response
content.comment:
Thank you for your response.

A1: I better understand your choice for the "mirror-like" term and the previous work you relied on. Since this was one of my primary concern, I will increase my rating of the paper. I still think that issues such as fertility and NULL alignments and how they are tackled, precisely, in your approach must be much more discussed to significantly improve the paper. Experiments on distant languages must be added.

A3: I understand but this is still supervised by sentence alignments. I don't really know since when using "unsupervised" for this scenario became acceptable. But I guess this is OK...

A4: Can we compare the computational cost using 1 CPU with using 1 GPU, fairly?  I am quite sure this is not that simple, especially because the price of buying and using 1 CPU is usually significantly smaller than for 1 GPU. The only way to fix this, and only if you want to make it a significant part your paper, would be to draw curves of computational times for using more and more CPUs/GPUs to see how they compare and analyse the results.


 A5: this is arguable, but this is just a minor comment.

A6: I understand, please add this explanation in the paper.

display_title: Interesting and efficient method, but missing strong baseline

content.title: Interesting and efficient method, but missing strong baseline
content.review:
This paper presents MirrorAlign, an intuitive and efficient method (as fast as fast-align) for word alignment given gold parallel sentences (bitext). The MirrorAlign model is built based on noise-contrastive estimation (Gutmann & Hyvarinen, 2010), while the intuition behind is that two words are likely to be aligned if they frequently appear in a pair of bitext. The authors also briefly show theoretical guarantee of the proposed method. 

While the idea is neat and the experiments are clear, this paper misses a strong baseline: \
SimAlign: High Quality Word Alignments without Parallel Training Data using Static and Contextualized Embeddings \
Masoud Jalili Sabet, Philipp Dufter, Hinrich Schutze \
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.08728.pdf

SimAlign is built upon XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT, which requires just separate monolingual corpora and sees no bitext, i.e., it requires less supervision than MirrorAlign; moreover, it achieves better alignment results on all investigated language pairs (de-en, en-fr, en-ro) than MirrorAlign. 

One can still argue that compare to SimAlign, MirrorAlign is much faster to train (assuming we have to pretrain large language models from scratch for SimAlign), but I doubt if we would really need that in real applications -- it is very convenient for people to apply pretrained language models nowadays. Another advantage of MirrorAlign is that it has much fewer parameters than previous models including SimAlign, but I am not sure if real applications would significantly benefit from such an advantage -- if so, it should be discussed more explicitly. 

Therefore, I stand in the middle between acceptance and rejection for this paper. 

## Detailed comments
- While I notice that the author(s) have added footnote 2 about Equation (6) and I can understand it, I would still appreciate it more if the equation is written in a more precise way. 
- I would rather not say that it is unfair to compare MirrorAlign with GIZA++ (and other models): the data availability for these models are the same, and we can definitely control the number of parameters, or tune it w.r.t. the development set -- both are approaches for fair comparison. When talking about fair comparison, my first impression is that models use different data and some uses more supervision than others, therefore the statements in the paper is perhaps misleading. 
- The reference needs some attention: there are duplicated items such as Stengel-Eskin et al. (EMNLP 2019) and Zenkel et al. (2020). 

## Questions
- Did you use any labeled dev set? If so, DE-EN does not have standard dev set, and I wonder what you used instead; if not, how did you select the best model for each method? 
- Did you train MirrorAlign for multiple times with different random seeds? If so, are the performances consistent?
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

replying_to: Replying to Interesting and efficient method, but missing strong baseline

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer #1
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments. We summarise and reply to your primary concerns as follows.

**Q1** SimAlign is built upon XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT, which requires just separate monolingual corpora and sees no bitext, i.e., it requires less supervision than MirrorAlign; moreover, it achieves better alignment results on all investigated language pairs (de-en, en-fr, en-ro) than MirrorAlign.

**A1** We noticed that your biggest concern is that missing comparison with the BERT-based models (mBERT & XLM), which achieve better performance than ours. I think this may be a common research concern in the field of NLP research recently. I will try to answer it from the following two perspectives：

- Industrially, although the pretraining model is already very popular, this type of BERT-based model is not easy to deploy online. Distillation or quantification are usually introduced to alleviate the efficiency issues. 

- Academically, I think it is unfair to evaluate a job only from the performance. Our model also has the potential to extend to a “deep” model or be equipped on some models for other tasks (e.g. NMT). 

Of course, we admit that the article you mentioned is very relevant to our research question. We will add SimAlign to give a good overview of neural alignment models. 

----

**Q2** Did you use any labeled dev set? If so, DE-EN does not have a standard dev set, and I wonder what you used instead; if not, how did you select the best model for each method?

**A2** No, we did not use a dev set for DE-EN. It is a pity that manual labeling of word alignments is costly and we only have a small published DE-EN test set. We follow the same experimental setup (https://github.com/lilt/alignment-scripts) as described by Zenkel et al. (2019) and Garg et al. (2019) to make a fair comparison. Namely, we all report the best results we achieved in the test set.

----

**Q3** Did you train MirrorAlign multiple times with different random seeds? If so, are the performances consistent?

**A3** Yes, we have trained MirrorAlign multiple times with different random seeds and the performances are consistent. The effect of our model can be affected by the hyperparameter(such as the alpha to balance two losses ), while the random seed has no obvious influence on the results.

content.title: Response to author reponse
content.comment:
Thanks for the response! 

Response to A1: I'm not trying to make the author(s) uncomfortable with pretrained models, however, there is no reason, except the potential computational efficiency problem, not to compare with pretrained models. If so, the distilled version of such models should be investigated and compared -- maybe MirrorAlign is still faster than them and competitively accurate. 

I definitely agree that MirrorAlign has the potential to extend to pretrained language models, however, it is not convincing enough if we only have feelings but not concrete results. 

Response to A2: I do feel a bit awkward to report the best test results, though previous work has done so -- imagine the extreme case, one can do random guess until they get out the test set perfectly -- I believe it's not the case for the paper (A3 has somewhat addressed my concern about this), but in the next version of this paper, I hope the author(s) could change it to a more standard setting in machine learning. 

Based on the current shape of the paper, I remain to give a rating of 5, and do not think it is strong enough to be published at ICLR.

content.title: An elegant method but not convincing enough
content.review:
This paper introduced a mechanism that applies cross lingual word embedding to the alignment task in machine translation. The authors proposed a training objective using parallel text -- they first use attention to obtain weightings of words, and obtain embeddings for the context (sentences) by weighted aggregation of individual token embeddings. They then used NCE training to maximize cosine similarity between positive examples, and at the same time, push away negative examples. By comparing this scheme with other alignment methods (Giza, Nnsa and naive attention), the author showed that their method has superior performance, and is faster.

The method is reasonable and the writing is clear. The primary concerns for me are the following:

1. The method seem to lack novelty. The mechanism is identical to what was originally proposed in the Seq2seq with attention model[Bahdanau 2014]. The authors takes the model, discarded the RNN component and then applied it to the alignment task. While there are several new components (NCE training objective and the "symmetric penalty"), they are not convincing enough to justify the novelty and contributions.

2. The evaluation is not convincing enough. Specifically, I would like to see comparisons with methods of similar nature -- for example, comparing with the alignment performance of a) the alignment produced by Seq2seq with attention model, and b) the "hard" alignment by using softmax on the cosine similarity of aligned bilingual embeddings. The overall method raises the speculation that the entire mechanism produces something similar to multilingual embeddings into one latent space (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.03652). As a result, comparisons with similar methodologies is crucial to show whether there are any distinctions or superiority. If one look at some anecdotal evidences (e.g. Fig 4), it seems that the the proposed method is "correct" because it does a better job in matching words with similar meanings -- this is achievable with lots of easier and more straightforward ways.

Despite my overall affection of simple and elegant solutions (and this paper definitely proposed one of them), I am not convinced by the potential contribution and the evaluations and there are room for improvements -- I vote for rejection.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer #3
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments. We summarise and reply to your primary concerns as follows.

**Q1:** Missing comparison with the alignment produced by Seq2seq with attention model.

**A1:** We will add (Bahdanau, 2014) to give a good overview of neural alignment models. However, we don't think we must make comparisons with that. As we mention in our paper, Koehn & Knowles (2017) show that attention mechanisms in the machine translation model dramatically diverge with word alignment. **Moreover, we also gave the results of that “naive attention” in Table-1, which is implemented based on a transformer-based seq2seq model and has a large performance margin with other methods.** We will highlight this in the next version to prevent such kind of misunderstanding.

----

**Q2:** Missing comparison with “hard” alignments inducted from Cross-lingual Word Embedding.

**A2:** To add comparisons with “straightforward” methods, such as using methods of Cross-lingual Word Embeddings(CWEs) or Bilingual Dictionary Induction(BDI), is an insightful perspective. As claimed in our paper, we also recognize our model as a pioneer attempt to unify bilingual word embedding and word alignments. 

However, what we want to draw your attention to is that the two tasks (CWEs and word alignment) have different research goals and scenarios essentially. CWEs focus on how to project monolingual word embeddings in the same latent space based on a given seed bilingual word dictionary(Mikolov et al., 2013, Artetxe et al., 2018) or even nothing(Cao et al., 2016, Zhang et al., 2017, Artetxe et al., 2017, Grave et al., 2019). **Namely, they usually do not consider the supervision signals at the parallel sentence level, as in the article you mentioned.** However, word alignment tasks focus on how to align words accurately between parallel sentences. CWEs are just the by-product of our model. In summary, we argue that simply introducing this type of method can not solve the word alignment problems, at least it won't be better.

Of course, we agree that adding such kinds of methods to compare with will make our article more convincing. We will explore it deeper, not only qualitatively, but also quantitatively analyze their differences, in future work.

----

**Q3:** Lacking novelty and room for improvements.

**A3:** For efficiency considerations, the context modeling for MirrorAlign is relatively simple, and only the pooling layer is used, which could be easily expanded. Some ideas for optimizing alignment in this article may also be applied to machine translation models. As a pioneer attempt to unify bilingual word embedding and word alignments, we believe it has potential for further research.

----

We keenly hope that you can re-evaluate our work based on our response.

content.title: Thank you for the comments.
content.comment:
This is to acknowledge that your response has been received.

I'm happy with the authors' response in A1.

My primacy question has not been addressed. Goals, scenarios, model details, etc. aside, the mechanism proposed in this paper, on a high level, raises the concern that what actually going on "under the hood" can be an implicit cross-lingual embedding of sorts -- learned from parallel text data. In essence, the proposed method takes word-level embeddings in one sentence, and calculate a softmax based on effectively cosine similarity to tokens in the target sequence. Using cosine similarity of cross-lingual embedding to obtain weighting schemes achieve something very close to it.

I'm hopeful to see if there are experiments and/or comparisons to prove otherwise -- but this part is missing. As I already mentioned, the anecdotal evidence given in the paper itself (fig 4) was suggesting that words of closer meanings are aligned to each other, which can be exactly achieved with cross-lingual embeddings.

"As claimed in our paper, we also recognize our model as a pioneer attempt to unify bilingual word embedding and word alignments." -- I would not suggest going that far. These concepts are not naturally separated at all. In most scenarios, they come together as by-products of various objectives, e.g. LMs, nnet-based machine translations. It's just in those cases, these by-products are sometimes not explicitly mentioned or analyzed. The architecture proposed in this paper is close to existing components in NMT.

display_title: Simple yet effective model for word alignment

content.title: Simple yet effective model for word alignment
content.review:
This paper proposed a lightweight unsupervised word alignment model that learns word alignment by encouraging the source and target words in parallel sentences to be close while pushing away irrelevant pairs.  The paper also introduces a disagree loss to encourage the attention from source to target to be symmetric with that from target to source, and thus learns more symmetric alignments. 

Strength:

1) The idea is intuitive and the proposed model is very efficient in training.
2) Added in extra loss to take care of the symmetric issue
3) Perform better than statistical methods on word alignment evaluations
4) Good ablation study and case analysis

Weakness:

1) Weak technical contribution
2) The notations can be more intuitive, for example,  you don't have to use both x_i and q_i to represent the source word vector just for showing that it's a query. 
3) It seems that your methods yield worse alignments than other more sophisticated neural network models. So what're the merits of having a more efficient but worse word alignment? Couldn't the users just compute the alignments offline? Perhaps you should give some use cases to show why your model can help users. Moreover, since more and more tasks are trained in an end-to-end fashion, less and less people are using word alignment for their tasks directly. Cao et al. (2019) https://openreview.net/forum?id=r1xCMyBtPS have shown that you can improve BERT's performance on downstream tasks with word alignment. It'll be better if you can show your alignment model can yield better results on downstream tasks.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer#2
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments. We summarize and reply to your questions as follows.

**Q1:** So what're the merits of having a more efficient but worse word alignment? Since more and more tasks are trained in an end-to-end fashion, fewer and fewer people are using word alignment for their tasks directly.

**A1:** Although the era of statistical machine translation has passed, there are still many industrial and academic demands for word alignment so that a fast model is needed. Word alignment is helpful for many downstream tasks. The most important application today for word alignments is to transfer text annotations from source to target (Mu ̈ller, 2017; Tezcan and Vandeghinste, 2011; Joanis et al., 2013; Escartın and Arcedillo, 2015). Even for NMT, word alignments are still useful for error analysis, inserting external vocabularies, and providing guidance for human translators in computer-aided translation. 

Stemming from efficiency, FastAlign is still one of the most popular words alignment tools now. Comparing to FastAlign, we achieve better performance and comparable efficiency so that we believe MirrorAlign has the potential to benefit both academia and industry.

----

**Q2:** The notations can be more intuitive. 

**A2:** Thank you for your detailed suggestions and we will adopt your suggestions in the final version of the paper.

content.title: response to the rebuttal
content.comment:
Thanks for the reply. 

For Q1, you changed my question, I didn't say "since more and more tasks are trained in an end-to-end fashion, fewer and fewer people are using word alignment for their tasks directly". My original concern is that user can compute the word alignment with a more complicated model but a much higher score offline, not end-to-end, in this case, you don't need efficiency. But sure, an efficient model with lower computational resources requirements can be useful some time.  Perhaps you can show that your model requires fewer parallel data to achieve better results. This could be very useful for low-resource languages.
